task.goal: Reduce double scans and missed scans at a small secondhand book sale checkout.
hard_constraints: One volunteer uses an existing barcode scanner and paper tally; no new software or paid hardware.
Do not retain buyer identities or slow the queue by more than a brief check per sale.
Compare both error types and checkout time over two sale sessions without claiming the sessions are identical.
task.available_resources: Scanner beep, printed item stickers, till receipts and a two-session paper tally.
task.expected_result: A reversible checkout procedure and an inspectable small trial.

DIRECT_FULL.title: One-way movement through the scanner
DIRECT_FULL.proposal: Use physical position as the record of progress. Keep unscanned books on one side of the scanner and completed books on the other. Pick up one book, present its barcode once, and move it across only after an accepted scan. Never return completed books to the input pile. This could reduce missed books and repeat presentations by making the next action visible rather than relying on memory. It needs enough counter space for two distinct piles and an existing way to correct accidental entries. A beep must reliably indicate an accepted entry; confirm this before relying on it. Interruptions, awkward stacks and automatic duplicate reads remain possible. No equipment or software changes are required, and the volunteer can abandon the layout immediately.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Across both sale sessions, alternate short blocks of the usual procedure and the two-pile procedure; reverse the starting order in session two. On a small, predetermined sample, pause before handing over the books and briefly compare each physical book with its receipt entry. This requires receipts with sufficiently identifiable entries; otherwise the available evidence cannot establish both error types independently. Record extra entries and missing entries separately, including errors corrected before payment, plus sampled checkout duration including the check. Use anonymous sale numbers and tally basket size, session and method. Compare errors per book and time per sale within each session, reporting sample counts and differences in basket sizes or workload. Reject or revise the procedure if errors do not decrease or the extra handling materially delays checkout. The audit itself may improve attention, so apply it equally to both methods.

DIRECT_FULL.title: A deliberate scan-and-confirm rhythm
DIRECT_FULL.proposal: Use a fixed attention sequence for each book: expose the barcode, present it once, withdraw it from the scanner's field, and acknowledge the acceptance beep before starting the next book. If no beep occurs, pause and deliberately retry that same book. This could prevent rapid repeat reads and omissions caused by moving on before acceptance. Unlike a counter layout, the mechanism is pacing each scanner interaction. It assumes the acceptance beep is audible and corresponds to a recorded entry; scanner sounds for rejection or other events must be distinguishable. It needs no extra materials and can be stopped immediately. It may offer little benefit if duplicate reads happen within a single presentation, and it could cost too much time on large baskets.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: In each of two sessions, alternate short blocks of ordinary scanning and the deliberate rhythm, starting with opposite methods in the second session. Sample sales by a rule fixed beforehand, such as every fifth sale. Briefly reconcile books against identifiable receipt entries before handover, applying the same inspection to both methods. Tally extra and missing entries separately, distinguishing errors caught during scanning from those found by inspection. Record basket size and elapsed checkout time, including confirmation and inspection, using an existing clock if available. Keep only anonymous transaction numbers. Inspect session-specific error counts per book and checkout time by basket size; do not treat the sessions as matched conditions. A useful falsifying result is unchanged errors with longer checkout, or continued repeat entries despite single presentations. If receipts cannot identify entries or no timing source exists, report those measurement limits rather than claiming verified error or time reductions.

DIRECT_FULL.title: A final count with targeted reconciliation
DIRECT_FULL.proposal: Before payment, compare the physical number of books with the number of book entries on the till receipt or existing transaction display. If they differ, reconcile entries against books and correct the sale before handover. This adds a brief independent check after scanning rather than changing scanning technique. It could catch either missing or duplicate entries while leaving most sales with only a count comparison. It assumes each book produces one identifiable entry, quantities are interpreted correctly, and non-book lines are excluded. Use the existing paper tally to record mismatches and corrections. No buyer details are needed, and the check is immediately reversible. Equal counts can conceal one missing book and one duplicate, so matching totals do not establish accuracy. Large baskets may also make counting too slow.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Alternate ordinary checkout and count-check blocks within each of two sessions, reversing the initial order in session two. For a small predetermined sample under both methods, briefly match every book to its receipt entry after the normal procedure, even when totals agree. This exposes offsetting errors that the count check misses. Record missing and extra entries separately, count-check corrections, residual errors found by the audit, basket size and total checkout duration including reconciliation. Use an existing clock for timing; without one, timing compliance remains unverified. Compare residual errors per book, correction frequency and time per sale within each session, noting queue pressure and basket-size differences. Do not pool the sessions as if identical. Reject the method if apparently matching counts often conceal errors, or mismatch investigations cause delays beyond the allowed brief check. Item-level verification depends on receipt detail; aggregate totals alone cannot validate both error types.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Make each book present only one readable barcode
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Before checkout, inspect the sale stickers and make the intended checkout barcode the only readable barcode on the book’s scanning face. Where spare printed item stickers are available and sufficiently opaque, use them to cover competing publisher, price or stock barcodes. Keep the intended barcode flat, fully visible and clear of adjacent covers. Do not cover information needed to price the book or place adhesive on a vulnerable book surface; leave unsuitable books unchanged.

The mechanism is removing competing scanner targets before the sale. This could reduce repeated presentations caused by reading an unintended code, and missed entries caused by an obscured or ambiguous intended code. It primarily addresses barcode presentation; whether that explains this sale’s errors is unknown. It will not prevent every repeated read or forgotten book.

This requires an identifiable intended barcode, spare suitable stickers and preparation time outside the queue. Confirm first that the scanner accepts representative prepared books. For reversibility, apply covers only to existing protective labels where they can be removed without damage. If that cannot be done with the available stickers, do not use this procedure.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment:
In each of two sessions, alternate short blocks using ordinary presentation and the single-barcode preparation, reversing the starting order in session two. Prepare books for intervention blocks before they reach checkout; record any books that cannot safely be prepared. Keep scanning practice otherwise unchanged.

For a small predetermined sample in both conditions, briefly match books against identifiable receipt entries before handover. Tally duplicate entries and missing entries separately, including corrections, plus book count and checkout duration using an existing clock if available. Retain only anonymous sale numbers. If receipt detail cannot distinguish books, both error types cannot be independently verified; if no clock is available, the time requirement remains unverified.

Compare errors per audited book and checkout time within each session, noting basket sizes and the proportion with competing barcodes. Report preparation effort separately. Reject the approach if errors persist at similar rates, preparation damages labels, or checkout checks exceed a brief pause. Treat session differences as context, not matched conditions.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Protect scanning from interruptions
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Treat scanning each sale as a short protected task. Before the first scan, resolve any visible price or sticker questions with a brief glance through the books. During scanning, defer conversation, change-making, sorting donations and questions about another sale until the current sale’s scanning is complete. If an interruption requires an immediate response, finish the current book’s accepted scan first. If the volunteer is already uncertain whether that book registered, check its receipt entry before presenting it again.

The mechanism is preventing task switches from erasing the volunteer’s memory of whether a scan happened. That uncertainty can cause either a retry that duplicates an entry or moving on with an unscanned book. This changes when competing tasks happen and requires no new equipment, software or buyer information. The volunteer can revert immediately.

It assumes interruptions contribute to errors, that ordinary questions can wait briefly, and that the existing till permits checking an uncertain entry. Confirm what the scanner beep means before treating it as acceptance. Urgent interruptions still take precedence. The procedure will have limited effect on automatic repeat reads or unreadable stickers; checking an ambiguous entry may also take too long.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment:
In each of two sale sessions, alternate short blocks of usual checkout and protected scanning, reversing the starting order in session two. Use the same brief receipt inspection on a predetermined small sample under both methods: match each book to an identifiable receipt entry before handover. Tally extra entries and missing entries separately, corrections, basket size, and whether scanning was interrupted. Use anonymous sale numbers only.

Measure checkout time from the first checkout action through handover, including preliminary questions and inspection, using an existing clock if available. Compare each method within each session, reporting sample sizes, interruptions and basket-size differences. Do not assume the sessions have equivalent customers or workload.

The smallest falsifying check is whether protected blocks actually reduce interruptions and whether audited errors fall without extending checkout beyond a brief additional check. Fewer interruptions with unchanged errors would weaken the proposed mechanism. Stop or revise if deferred questions cause longer delays. If receipt detail cannot distinguish books, both error types cannot be verified independently; without a timing source, the time constraint remains unverified.

EXPAND.title: Expose only the sale barcode
EXPAND.proposal:
Prevent ambiguous reads before scanning. At checkout, position each book so that only its sale barcode faces the scanner. Where publisher, warehouse or old shop barcodes compete with the sale sticker, use an available printed sticker to cover the competing code temporarily, without attaching anything to bare or fragile book surfaces. Leave the intended barcode completely readable. Scan normally, complete payment and hand over the books; remove temporary covers if needed. The mechanism is controlling which code the scanner can acquire, addressing wrong-code reads and repeated attempts caused by competing labels.

The checkout volunteer owns the procedure. It requires spare stickers, clearly recognizable sale barcodes and a safe way to cover competing codes. First inspect several books: if they already have only one readable barcode, this route has little justification. It will not prevent repeated reads of the correct code or omissions unrelated to label confusion. Compared with the prior scan-and-confirm rhythm, it changes the scanner's input rather than the volunteer's pacing. Stop using covers if positioning or removal becomes lengthy, damages labels or obscures sale information.
EXPAND.experiment:
In each of two sessions, alternate small blocks of ordinary checkout and controlled barcode exposure, reversing the starting order in session two. Include preparation and cover removal in checkout time. On a predetermined small sample under both methods, briefly match physical books to identifiable receipt entries before handover; record missing entries, duplicate entries and wrong-item entries separately, including corrections. Record anonymous sale number, book count, competing-barcode presence, method and duration on paper.

Use an existing clock or sufficiently precise receipt timestamps if available; otherwise time compliance remains unverified. Receipt detail must support item matching; totals alone cannot validate both errors. Compare error rates and time within each session, especially among books with competing labels, without treating sessions as identical. Stop after a short initial block if covering adds more than the permitted brief check. No improvement over ordinary checkout, or over the prior rhythm when label confusion is present, would undermine the mechanism.

EXPAND.title: Close the basket before opening the sale
EXPAND.proposal:
Make the set of books stable while the volunteer records it. Before scanning, ask the buyer to place all selected books on the counter and confirm that the selection is complete. Then scan and pay for that set without accepting additions, removals or rearrangement by the buyer. Handle a late addition as a separate sale after the first receipt; process a withdrawal using the till's existing correction procedure before payment. Hand over the completed set with its receipt.

The mechanism is preventing the physical basket from changing while the transaction is being assembled. Late additions, books taken back for inspection and partially scanned books returned by a buyer can create both omissions and repeated scans. This differs from the prior two-pile layout: it controls changes at the transaction boundary rather than representing progress through a fixed pile.

The volunteer owns the rule and explains it in one short sentence. It requires room to present a whole basket and an existing correction method. It assumes basket changes occur often enough to matter. It cannot address scanner-generated duplicates or failures within an otherwise stable basket. Separate sales may increase receipt use, payment overhead or confusion; abandon the procedure when those costs outweigh the brief initial confirmation.
EXPAND.experiment:
Across two sessions, alternate short blocks of usual checkout and closed-basket checkout, reversing the initial order in session two. On a small predetermined sample, briefly reconcile books against identifiable receipt entries before handover under both methods. Record omissions and duplicates separately, corrections, basket changes and anonymous basket size.

Measure total service time for the buyer's entire purchase, including any second transaction, using an existing timing source if available. Count extra receipts and withdrawal corrections as shifted costs. Without adequate timing or identifiable receipt entries, report the respective measurement limit.

Compare errors per book and service time within each session, recording queue pressure rather than assuming comparable sessions. The strongest relevant comparator is the prior two-pile procedure: a later small comparison should determine whether freezing the basket adds value beyond visible scan progress. Stop during the first block if separate transactions repeatedly extend service beyond a brief check. Unchanged errors accompanied by more transactions would falsify the practical benefit.

EXPAND.title: Replace individual scans with grouped price quantities where already supported
EXPAND.proposal:
Work backward from the required sale total: if the existing till already accepts a price category and quantity, individual barcode acquisition may be unnecessary for books with clearly printed prices. The volunteer reads the price stickers, groups books by price, counts each group and enters one quantity for each price using the till's existing controls. The receipt then states category quantities and totals. Complete payment and hand over the books. Use normal scanning for an entire basket whenever a sticker is ambiguous, an exception requires item identification or grouping would be cumbersome.

This removes repeated scanner interactions rather than improving their execution. It could eliminate scanner omissions and duplicate reads in eligible baskets, but counting, price selection and quantity-entry mistakes can recreate equivalent missing or extra charges. Those errors must count against the proposal.

The volunteer owns a narrowly bounded trial, initially restricted to small baskets with one clearly marked price. Prerequisites are existing manual quantity entry, permission under the sale's normal accounting rules to use category receipts, and no requirement for item-level inventory records. Inspect these prerequisites before trying the method; do not change software or invent a manual-entry facility. Printed stickers, receipts and the paper tally provide the remaining materials. If any prerequisite fails, this alternative is unavailable. Return immediately to scanning when eligibility is uncertain or a correction cannot be completed promptly.
EXPAND.experiment:
In both sessions, alternate eligible baskets between usual scanning and grouped quantity entry, reversing the starting assignment in session two. Keep ineligible baskets outside the comparison and tally their frequency to show the method's limited coverage.

For a predetermined small sample, independently recount books by sticker price and compare the result with receipt quantities before handover. Record under-recorded and over-recorded quantities separately, plus wrong-price entries and corrections. Apply equivalent brief inspection to scanned baskets; identifiable receipt entries or price quantities are necessary for that comparison. Record anonymous basket size, preparation time, entry time and correction time using an existing timing source; without one, the time constraint cannot be verified.

Compare both error directions and total checkout time within each session, acknowledging differing baskets and conditions. The prior two-pile scan procedure is the strongest relevant alternative because it retains item scanning with little added work. Stop if grouped entry exceeds a brief additional check, introduces unresolved accounting discrepancies or merely trades scanning errors for quantity or price errors. Fewer scanner mistakes alone would not establish success.

EXPAND.title: One-way scanning with an explicit interruption recovery
EXPAND.proposal: Upgrade the one-way movement route, the strongest direct fit because it makes scan progress visible with little routine work. The volunteer keeps unscanned books on one side and accepted books on the other, presenting one book once and moving it only after confirmed acceptance. The changed action addresses an interruption while a book is between piles: put that book separately and resolve its recorded status before scanning anything else. Check the existing till's latest entry if it identifies that book; move it to the completed pile if recorded, or scan it if absent. Never guess or automatically rescan an uncertain book. This requires counter space, a verified acceptance beep, an existing correction procedure and a usable way to inspect the current transaction. If transaction inspection is unavailable, use the ordinary correction procedure and discontinue this upgraded route. The volunteer retains responsibility until books and receipt are handed over. Compared with the original layout, this may prevent interruption-induced duplicates or omissions, but adds a check on interrupted sales and cannot prevent automatic duplicate reads. Revert immediately if recovery is ambiguous or routinely exceeds a brief check.
EXPAND.experiment: Before the sale, inspect beep meaning, transaction visibility and correction controls using the existing equipment without creating an unreconciled sale. In each of two sessions, alternate short blocks of ordinary checkout and the upgraded procedure; reverse the starting method in session two. The volunteer audits a predetermined small sample equally under both methods by briefly matching books to identifiable receipt entries before handover. Tally missing and duplicate entries separately, corrections during scanning, residual errors, interruptions, basket size and anonymous sale number. Measure total checkout time including recovery and audit using an existing clock or sufficiently precise receipt timestamps; if neither exists, the required time comparison cannot be completed with the supplied resources. Likewise, insufficient receipt detail prevents verification of both error types. Begin with one short block and stop if checks or recoveries exceed the agreed brief-check allowance. Compare errors per audited book and checkout time by basket size within each session, describing queue pressure and other differences between sessions. Do not claim the sessions are equivalent or count corrected errors as residual errors.

EXPAND.title: Count-check checkout with a bounded mismatch recovery
EXPAND.proposal: Upgrade the final-count route, a competitive mechanism because it checks the completed transaction independently of scanning technique. The volunteer compares physical book count with receipt book quantity, excluding non-book lines and expanding quantity entries correctly. Preserve the source's targeted book-to-entry reconciliation when counts disagree. The changed action is an explicit recovery boundary: attempt one direct correction only when the discrepant book and entry are unambiguous. If they are not, use the till's existing cancel-and-restart procedure once for a small basket, provided that facility has been verified and restarting fits the brief-check allowance. On restart, scan the intact basket from the beginning and repeat the count. Never add or delete an arbitrary entry merely to make totals agree. If cancellation is unavailable, a restart remains ambiguous, or the time allowance would be exceeded, return to the sale's ordinary correction procedure and stop using this intervention. The volunteer owns the check and recovery before handover. This needs only the scanner, receipts and paper tally, but depends on readable book quantities and existing correction controls. Compared with count checking alone, the recovery rule may limit speculative corrections and prolonged searching; restarting adds work and can introduce fresh errors. Equal counts still conceal offsetting omissions and duplicates.
EXPAND.experiment: First inspect whether receipts distinguish book quantities and whether an unpaid transaction can be safely cancelled and restarted. Restrict the initial intervention block to small baskets whose restart could plausibly fit the brief-check allowance; record this eligibility limit. Across two sessions, alternate ordinary checkout and the upgraded count check in short blocks, reversing the starting order in session two. On a predetermined small sample under both methods, briefly match every physical book to its identifiable receipt entry, including when counts agree. Record missing and duplicate entries separately, errors corrected by the count check, residual audit errors, restarts, failed recoveries, basket size and total checkout time including all corrections and inspection. Use anonymous sale numbers. Timing requires an existing clock or sufficiently precise receipt timestamps; item-level auditing requires adequate receipt detail. If either prerequisite fails, report that the full trial cannot establish the required outcome. Stop after the first short block if recovery exceeds the brief-check allowance or creates unresolved entries. Compare both error rates and time within each session and by basket size, documenting differences in workload between sessions. Matching counts alone, fewer scanner retries, or errors shifted into restart transactions do not establish success.
